To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) there is a significant positive relationship between publication and student ratings of teaching; (ii) there is no relationship between quality of publication and student ratings; (iii) there is a relationship between publication and evaluation by colleagues; (iv) there is no difference between quality of publication of those teachers whose colleagues rated them highly and those whose colleagues rated them less highly.
(1) a person's effectiveness as a teacher is not significantly related to his research publication record and (2) his effectiveness is significantly related to his students' ratings of his teaching.

(1) the more a faculty member publishes in scholarly journals, the higher the rating he gets from his colleagues; (2) the more he publishes, the more favorable the rating he gets on his teaching effectiveness from a sample of his students; (3) the more he writes, the more favorable is the rating he receives from a sample of students who are not his own, and who have not taken any of his courses, but who are representative of the student population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between publication record of faculty members and the effectiveness of their teaching as estimated from student evaluations.
the relationship between publication record of college teachers and effectiveness of teaching as measured by the students' evaluations of the teachers' performances in the classroom.
a comparison of the teaching effectiveness of persons who publish much, those who publish a moderate amount, and those who do not publish much or at all.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a relationship between publication record of faculty members and their teaching effectiveness as estimated by a representative sample.
